chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
title: Rehearsing Cab's reeds and rebuilding the band
summary: Working with Hilton Jefferson-era sidemen, McRae called section rehearsals and Cab's sections began to play better.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: then I began to get with (inaudible) Jeff who was a good friend of mine. He had played with us -- with Chick.
And Jeff was over there, he was glad to see me. He come over, you know, because (inaudible). They needed somebody to play that sheet.
Chu was a great soloist, but he used to lay back and wait for his solo. And Cab asked me, "All that stuff you playing is down on that sheet?"
I say, "Yeah, every bit is down there."
"I never heard none of that."

I say, "Well, you know, because Chu sits up and wait for his solo, Cab. You know how Chu is. Sit up there with his big fat self and wait for the solos, think he's the greatest thing in the world, you know."
And the guys (inaudible). I say, "Well, you know, (inaudible) Chu." Great man, I love him. He used to play good, you know.
So when I come in the band, I started getting with Jeff. I say, "Look, I don't know your book."

Cab's got that little funny stomp-off he does. One, two, three -- when you hit on five, I say, "Now I hit out there."

I says, "I tell you what you do. Why don't we call a little rehearsal so we can get together and straighten out our vibratos (inaudible), our blend together and work on, (inaudible) clean up the arrangements. You got little spots here -- you got little trickie things I ain't never played, you know."
And we worked it out. And we began to get together, and the band began to come to some kind of life, because the trombones and the trumpets began to do the same thing we did.
And the band was coming to life with Cab.
And when we came back to New York at the Strand Theater, Cab Calloway had one of the best sounding bands he ever had.
Because I really got in there and we went to work. One or two little things that I suggested --
Jonah Jones was in the band. And he
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
say, "Oh, man, (look out inaudible) we got you here now, man."
I say, "Look, let's clean this band up instead of waiting here for a payday. It don't make sense."
I say, "Look, there's a little few things that I don't know, and you got some good things here, if we just put them together -- we work on them."

So we -- the saxophone players, there's Walter Thomas, and Jeff and myself -- we started cleaning that section out. Got that section sounding big and strong. And they sound like a saxophone section. Everybody playing, you know.
The trumpet players started taking a little break after shows and getting together and cleaning up their book.
And the trombones (inaudible) -- and Tyree and them, they started doing the same thing. Jonah Jones and them was in there. They wasn't doing nothing but sitting up there waiting for a payday.
I say, "Yall waiting for a payday."
I say, "Man, yall could add a little

something in there. Little riffs in there." So we started rehearsing, you know. Cab say, "All you band leaders are taking over my band." He used to kid us like that, you know. I say, "Oh no, come on. We're just trying"-- I say, "Look, I'm new in the band, right? So I had to ask Jeff to call rehearsal so I could clean it up. He sitting up going over the same thing I'm missing." So I say, "I don't know that," you know, "doing Cherokee and they show me what they do with that." And the first night I played it, Jeff told me -- he say, "Now look, when we go and hit this Cherokee, the band play the first chorus and we go back, make a modulation and you got it, you made-like blow. (inaudible) Chu Berry, you blow." 'Chu Berry's thing. So we play it all the way through. When it get back to you -- next time they play, don't go back to the middle part. Just
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
keep on playing sixteen bars, sixteen bars (inaudible)." And it was a great arrangement. And two weeks I was in the band, the band began to take new life, new shape.
Because we were rehearsing after every first show. We have the second show -- We go down the basement, the (inaudible) saxophone, we would rehearse. And we would clean --

Cab had a lot of good music. And we began to play other things that Cab hadn't played. "Hey, Cab, we play so and so and so." And we played it and it sound -- Cab say, "Yeah," -- and he'd be callin' them... (inaudible), you know. Because it was a lot of things -- They would just play the same thing that Cab play. And during rehearsal with Jeff and the reed section, it was other things in the book. I say, "Hey, Cab, would you play so and so." They wouldn't (inaudible). I'd tell him (inaudible). Cab say -- I say, "Oh yeah, you can talk to Cab. I tell him, I say, "Look, hey, Cab, why don't
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
you play that arrangement today. (Inaudible) that's a good arrangement." And he began to play different arrangements instead of calling the same set every night.
They would let him call what he wanted, because -- all right, the man got a lot on his mind, he don't think of all those songs and the arrangements in the book.
So I begin to tell him, "Hey, Cab, play so and so. Play number so and so."
Then Jonah say, "Yeah, let's play so and so." Everybody started coming out calling different numbers.
Then we got into something real good. And the band -- I liked the band. I stayed with them for about two years.
